entities.name: Callicratidas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Callicratidas, a Spartan nauarch (admiral), commanded the Lacedaemonian fleet during a critical phase of the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE), specifically in 406–405 BCE. His tenure marked a period of renewed Spartan naval aggression against Athens following the recall of the highly successful but controversial Lysander. Callicratidas’s leadership represented a return to traditional Spartan values, emphasizing self-reliance and honor over the diplomatic maneuvering and personal ambition that characterized some of his predecessors.

Taking command in 406 BCE, Callicratidas quickly secured Persian financial support from Cyrus the Younger, though not without friction, which was vital for maintaining the large Spartan fleet. His strategic objective was to decisively defeat the Athenian navy. He achieved a significant initial success by blockading the Athenian general Conon and his fleet in the harbor of Mytilene on Lesbos. This action severely threatened Athens’ supply lines and its capacity to wage war, forcing the Athenians to mount a massive, hastily assembled relief effort, which included arming slaves.

The ensuing Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE, fought off the coast of Lesbos, became one of the largest naval engagements of the ancient world. Despite Callicratidas's personal bravery and leadership, the Spartan fleet suffered a catastrophic defeat at the hands of the Athenian relief force, and Callicratidas himself perished in the battle. His death, coupled with the loss of 70 Spartan ships and thousands of men, momentarily reversed Spartan gains and led to the infamous trial of the victorious Athenian generals for failing to rescue shipwrecked sailors, an event that further destabilized Athenian politics.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Callicratidas's command represented a crucial, albeit brief, phase in the Peloponnesian War, directly leading to one of its largest naval battles and influencing the subsequent political turmoil in Athens. His death cleared the path for Lysander's return, which ultimately sealed Athens' defeat.
